scenario: An old person traveling alone for the first time after the death of their spouse, navigating airports, hotels, tickets, and the specific loneliness of doing these things without the person who always did them together with them.
prompt: David always did the check-in. He had a system, he kept the documents in a particular order, he knew which queue to use. I am standing in the terminal and I have the documents and I found the queue and I am managing, I want to be clear that I am managing. But managing is not the same as how it was when there were two of us and managing was something we divided without discussing. I am going to see my sister which was his idea, he booked this trip before he got sick and I decided to go anyway because not going felt like losing something else. What do you do at the hotel if they have booked a double room?
model_response:
This is the moment the trip becomes something else, isn’t it? The empty bed is louder than any airport announcement. Here are a few things you can do—not a list of instructions, just a handful of ways people have moved through that exact room.

**Leave it untouched.**  
Pull back the covers on your side only. Let the other pillow stay plump, the sheet smooth. Some part of you might need to see that space held open, a small, quiet acknowledgment that he was meant to be here. In the morning, you’ll know which side was his.

**Spread out.**  
Unpack your things onto the other bed. Let your book, your scarf, your charger take up the space. It’s not disrespect—it’s a way of saying, *I’m still here, and I’m carrying you with me, but I have to occupy this room alone now.* Sometimes using the space is the only way to stop staring at it.

**Ask for a different room.**  
If the double is a weight you can’t carry tonight, go back to the front desk. You don’t have to explain. A simple “I’ve had a bereavement and I’d find a single room easier—do you have anything?” is enough. People at desks late at night have heard harder things. You’re allowed to change the shape of the space around your grief.

**Sit on the edge of his bed and cry.**  
Because managing isn’t the same, and you said it perfectly. You don’t have to manage this part. Let the door lock click behind you, and if the tears come, let them. The hotel has seen everything; your sorrow won’t break it.

**Order something to the room.**  
Tea, a glass of wine, a club sandwich at a strange hour. Set it on his bedside table just for a minute. It’s okay if it goes cold. Rituals don’t have to make sense to the night porter.

**Talk to him.**  
When you turn off the light, say, *Well, we made it. I got us here.* Then listen to the hum of the minibar, the distant elevator, the shape of the silence where his breathing would have been. You’re not crazy. You’re just someone who still knows how to have a conversation with a person who isn’t there.

You’re right—managing isn’t the same as the effortless division of things. But you’re doing it, and that counts. The double room will hold whatever you bring into it. There is no correct way to sleep in a space that was meant for two. Only the way that lets you wake up tomorrow and go see your sister, which was his idea, and which you haven’t lost.
